```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(statmodels7)
set.seed(1)
```

An ordinary regression models the mean and treats everything else about the
distribution as a nuisance held constant. A distributional model gives every
parameter its own equation, so the scale, the shape and a zero-inflation
probability may each depend on covariates, and each may be a smooth, a random
effect or a penalized block.

`statmod()` reads one formula that carries all of them, in which a bar
separates the equations, and fits it. This vignette walks through a fit and then through the
functions that read it.

```{r}
n <- 300
da <- data.frame(x = sort(runif(n, min = -3, max = 3)))
da$y <- rnorm(n, mean = 1 + 0.8 * da$x, sd = exp(-0.6 + 0.35 * da$x))
```

The scale of these data grows with `x`, from about $0.19$ at $x = -3$ to about
$1.57$ at $x = 3$.

## A first fit

The first equation belongs to the first parameter of the distribution, so a
formula with no bar models the mean and leaves the other parameters as
intercepts:

```{r}
f1 <- statmod(y ~ x, distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), data = da)
coef(f1)
```

`coef()` returns one compartment per parameter, because the coefficients of
the mean and of the scale are different quantities on different scales, and a
single flat vector would run them together. For this model the compartment of
the mean holds the coefficients of an ordinary regression, which the following
check confirms:

```{r}
all.equal(unname(coef(f1)$mu), unname(coef(lm(y ~ x, data = da))),
          tolerance = 1e-6)
```

## Modeling the scale

A parameter is named on the left of its own equation, after a bar:

```{r}
f2 <- statmod(y ~ x | sigma ~ x, distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), data = da)
lapply(coef(f2), round, digits = 3)
```

The truth is $\mu = 1 + 0.8x$ and $\log\sigma = -0.6 + 0.35x$. The equation of
the scale is on the log scale, which is the link of that parameter: an
equation is fitted on the scale that keeps its parameter inside its domain, so
a combination of covariates cannot produce a negative standard deviation.

The log-likelihoods of the two fits show the gain from the second equation:

```{r}
c(constant_scale = loglik(f1), modeled_scale = loglik(f2))
```

## Terms

Any `modelterms7` term goes in any equation. A smooth carries a penalty, and its
smoothing parameter is estimated from the data:

```{r}
db <- data.frame(z = sort(runif(n, min = -3, max = 3)),
                 g = factor(rep(1:20, length.out = n)))
db$y <- rnorm(n, mean = 1 + sin(1.4 * db$z) + rnorm(20, sd = 0.6)[db$g], sd = 0.4)

f3 <- statmod(y ~ s(z, bspline_smooth(k = 8)),
              distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), data = db)
f3@edf
```

The smooth has `r f3@edf$coefficients[2]` coefficients and uses about
`r round(f3@edf$edf[2], 1)` of them. This effective number of degrees of
freedom is the one that a criterion counts, in place of the number of coefficients.
`hyper()` reports the hyperparameters and the source of each:

```{r}
hyper(f3)
```

A random effect is written the same way and is fitted by the same machinery,
and its penalty is a Gaussian prior over the group effects:

```{r}
f4 <- statmod(y ~ s(z, bspline_smooth(k = 8)) + random(~ 1 | g),
              distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), data = db)
f4@edf
hyper(f4)
```

The 20 group effects spend about `r round(f4@edf$edf[3], 1)` degrees of freedom
here, and the estimated prior scale is `r round(hyper(f4)$estimate[2], 2)`,
against the 0.6 used to draw the groups. A random intercept is a ridge
penalty on an indicator block, so it is fitted like a smooth.

## Who chooses the hyperparameters

Every hyperparameter is estimated unless the term holds it. The criterion
is set by the arguments `outer_criterion` and `sparse_criterion` of
`statmod()`. The argument `outer_criterion` applies to the
hyperparameters of a penalty that is twice differentiable, such as a smooth or a
random effect:

* `reml()` and `ml()` are marginal criteria. They integrate out the penalized
  coefficients and are differentiable, so the search uses an exact gradient and,
  where it exists, an exact Hessian. `reml()` is the default.
* `aic()` and `bic()` score an estimate of prediction error instead.

A penalty with a kink (`lasso()`, `enet()`, `scad()` and `mcp()`) is chosen
along a path of its own values, from the value that empties the block
downwards, and the path is scored by `sparse_criterion`. This argument is
`bic()` by default and may be `aic()` or `cv()`, and a marginal criterion is
rejected there. A marginal criterion expands the penalized objective around the
penalized mode, and for a lasso that mode lies *at* the kink, where the second
derivative does not exist. The function `cv()` serves only as
`sparse_criterion`.

A term holds a hyperparameter when the call names its value, for example
`lasso(x, lambda = 3)` or `s(z, bspline_smooth(k = 8), hyper = c(lambda = 2))`,
and the `held` column of `hyper()` then reports `TRUE`:

```{r}
f5 <- statmod(y ~ s(z, bspline_smooth(k = 8), hyper = c(lambda = 2)),
              distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), data = db)
hyper(f5)
```

## Reading a fit

```{r}
summary(f3)
```

The log-likelihood is the
conditional one, read at the fitted coefficients, and the effective degrees
of freedom go with it: `cAIC` and `cBIC` are built from that pair, and comparing
a conditional log-likelihood with a marginal one from another package compares
two different quantities. The interval of a hyperparameter, such as a smoothing
parameter or a prior standard deviation, is built on the scale that keeps it
positive and mapped back, so it cannot contain a negative number, while the
interval of a coefficient is on the link scale of its equation. The last lines,
headed `inner` and `outer`, give the largest gradient in standard errors and the
smallest eigenvalue of the curvature for the coefficients and for the
hyperparameters, and both are read at the point that the fit reached.

## The certificate

The convergence flag of an optimizer records whether a stopping rule fired.
`statmod_certificate()` tests a different property: whether the point reported
is a mode of the penalized objective and a stationary point of the criterion in
the hyperparameters.

```{r}
cert <- statmod_certificate(f4)
c(state = cert$state, mode_error = signif(cert$mode_error, digits = 3))
```

`mode_error` is how far above its own penalized mode the inner fit stopped, in
log-likelihood units, so one limit serves every model whatever its scale. The
`state` is `converged`; `boundary`, where a hyperparameter or an estimated
coefficient lies at an edge of its range with the criterion flat in it, or the
outer curvature has a flat direction; `not converged`; or `unknown`, where the
derivatives that the certificate needs cannot be computed.

## Prediction, and the ordinary generics

`predict()` returns one compartment per parameter, with a standard error on
request:

```{r}
nd <- data.frame(z = c(-1, 0, 1),
                 g = factor(c(1, 2, 3), levels = levels(db$g)))
predict(f4, newdata = nd, se = TRUE)$mu
```

Prediction reapplies each term's `build_info` instead of rebuilding it, so the
knots of a smooth and the levels of a factor are those of the fitted model. As a
consequence, predicting at rows that were used to fit the model returns the
fitted values there.

The generics of `stats` apply to a fit:

```{r}
c(nobs = nobs(f4), df.residual = df.residual(f4))
length(sigma(f4))
```

`sigma()` returns the standard deviation of the response at each observation, so
it is a vector wherever the scale is modeled or the variance depends on the
mean. `df.residual()` subtracts the *effective* count of degrees of freedom from
the number of observations, so it is not an integer.

Three generics signal an error, and each error message names the function to
use instead.
`terms()` fails because a fit has one set of terms per distribution parameter,
`model.frame()` fails because a fit keeps the `build_info` of each term and not the
data, and `anova()` fails because a penalized fit whose hyperparameters were
chosen from the same data has no null distribution against which to test.

## Simulating from a model

`rstatmod()` draws from a model at coefficients supplied by the caller, as a
simulation study needs:

```{r}
sim <- rstatmod(y ~ x, distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), data = da,
                par = list(mu = c(1, 0.8), sigma = -0.6))
names(sim)
head(sim$data, n = 3)
```

It returns the true parameters beside the data and not as an attribute of the
data. An attribute survives a row subset without being subset itself, so if the
parameters were stored in `attr(sim$data, "theta")`, the result of
`attr(sim$data[1:10, ], "theta")` would still hold every row's parameters and
would be misaligned with the rows kept.

## Summary

* One formula, in which the equations are separated by a bar, one per
  distribution parameter; an equation that is omitted is an intercept.
* Each equation is fitted on the link scale of its parameter, so a combination
  of covariates cannot leave the domain of the parameter.
* `coef()`, `predict()` and `summary()` return one compartment per parameter.
* Any `modelterms7` term goes in any equation, and its penalty travels with it.
* Hyperparameters are estimated unless a term holds one: by `reml()` or `ml()`
  (or `aic()` or `bic()`) as `outer_criterion` where the penalty is twice
  differentiable, and along a path scored by `sparse_criterion` (`bic()` by
  default, or `aic()` or `cv()`) where it has a kink.
* The log-likelihood reported is the conditional one, and `cAIC` and `cBIC` use
  the effective degrees of freedom and not a parameter count.
* `statmod_certificate()` tests whether the point is a mode of the model, which
  the flag of the optimizer does not do.
